Victoria,

This is a
forum non conveniens

application.

The defendant applies for an
order that this court decline jurisdiction to entertain the plaintiff's liable
action and to enter a stay of proceedings pursuant to Rule 14(6)(c) in s. 8 of
the
Law and Equity Act
R.S.B.C. (1979), c. 224.

Rule 14 provides:

(6)Where
a person is served with an originating process has not entered an appearance
and alleges that:

(c)the
court has no jurisdiction over him in the proceeding or should decline
jurisdiction, the person may apply to the court for a declaration to that
effect.

The relevant section of the
Law
and Equity Act
is:

8.   No
cause or proceeding pending in the court shall be restrained by prohibition or
injunction; but every matter of equity on which an injunction against the
prosecution of that cause or proceeding might have been obtained before April
29, 1879, either conditionally or unconditionally, may be relied on by way of
defence.  Nothing in this
Act
shall disable the court from directing a
stay of proceedings in any cause or matter pending before it if it thinks fit
and any person, whether a party or not to that cause or matter, who would have
been entitled, but for this
Act
, to apply to the court to restrain the
prosecution of it, or who may be entitled to enforce, by attachment or
otherwise, any judgment, decree, rule or order, contrary to which all or any
part of the proceedings in the cause or matter have been taken, is at liberty
to apply to the court, by motion in a summary way, for a stay of proceedings in
the cause or matter, either generally or so far as may be necessary for the
purposes of justice.  The court shall make any order as is just.

On November 9, 1990 the plaintiff
issued a writ of summons with a Statement of Claim attached.  In the Statement
of Claim, the plaintiff is described as, "... a well known author and
historian who has published many books on the history of the 2nd World
War."  The plaintiff alleges in the statement of claim that the defendant,
a minister of the federal Crown, namely, the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship,
defamed the plaintiff by issuing a written statement on the defendant's
personal behalf and in the defendant's position as a Federal Cabinet Minister.

The statement is as follows:

a
BC-sec-state-statement 10-26 0264

News
release via Canada NEWSWire, Ottawa 613-563-4465

Attention:  News Editors

STATEMENT
BY THE HONOURABLE GERRY WEINER ON SPEAKING TOUR OF DAVID IRVING

OTTAWA
- The right to freedom of speech is central to our notion of Canada as a free
society.  It is a tremendous responsibility, therefore, for any one, in
particular a Minister of the Crown, to question the right of any individual to
express his or her beliefs or opinions in public.

I
am, however, both as a private citizen and as the Federal Minister responsible
for Human Rights, extremely disquieted by the speaking tour starting this
weekend by British writer David Irving.

David
Irving has made a career out of writing and lecturing that the Nazi persecution
of Jews and the Holocaust itself have been exagerated (sic).  He has given
support to and received sponsorship from individuals and organizations whose
racist and anti-semitic credentials are beyond dispute.  He has testified in
court on behalf of Ernst Zundel who was subsequently found guilty under
Canada's laws against the promotion of hatred.

Mr.
Irving's sympathies and intentions have no place in our society.  They are
abhorrent to Canadian values and ideals and are an incitement to racism if not
a direct promotion of racist attitudes.  I believe the vast majority of
Canadians join me in expressing to Mr. Irving our complete and utter rejection
of his pseudo-historic theories and the web of myths and distortions by which
he seeks to obscure the full horror and inhumanity of the Nazi regime.

For
further information:  Len Westerberg, Office of the Honourable Gerry Weiner,
(819) 997-7788.

It is alleged in paragraph 5 of
the Statement of Claim which is not disputed:

5.   The
foregoing article was distributed by the defendant to an organization known as
Canadian Newswire at Ottawa, which the defendant knew, or ought to have known,
would be distributed to every media outlet in the country upon release to the
aforesaid wire service.

The following paragraphs are
taken from the defendant's chambers brief supported by affidavit material filed
with respect to the motion:

4.Canada
Newswire distributed the written statement to 222 news media subscribers
throughout Canada, including 25 in British Columbia and 69 in Ontario.

5.In
addition, the Department of Secretary of State requested distribution of the
written statement on October 30, 1990 to ethnic print, newspaper, T.V. and
radio as well as various ethnocultural organizations throughout Canada,
totalling 2,147 including 935 in Ontario and 160 in British Columbia.

6.The
Plaintiff David Irving is and was at all material times to this action a
resident of the City of London in the United Kingdom.  In the fall of 1990 the
Plaintiff arranged a cross-Canada speaking tour.  The tour was scheduled to
begin in Victoria, British Columbia on October 27, 1990 and to end in Toronto,
Ontario on November 8, 1990.

7.The
Defendant resides in Quebec and maintains a temporary residence in Ottawa,
Ontario in order to fulfill his duties and responsibilities as a member of
Parliament and a Minister of the federal Crown.  By virtue of his position the
Defendant is required to attend regular sittings in the House of Commons as a
Member of Parliament and to respond to questions in the House of Commons
addressed to the Minister of the Department of Multiculturalism and
Citizenship.  The Defendant is also required on a regular basis to attend
meetings of the Priorities and Planning Committee of Cabinet.  The Defendant
also has the responsibility of the management and direction of the Department
of Multiculturalism and Citizenship which includes regular meetings in Hull and
Ottawa with his Deputy Minister, other departmental officials and individuals,
in order to take decisions emanating from the Defendant's responsibilities.
Further, the Defendant must be available at both his Ottawa and Hull offices to
meet with individuals and groups from across Canada in matters relating to
carrying out his duties as a Minister of the federal Crown and as a member of
Parliament.  Further, as the Defendant is a member of the House of Commons
representing the constituency of Pierrefonds-Dollard Des Ormeaux, in Quebec,
when Parliament is in session, he is usually in his riding to fulfill his
constituency responsibilities on weekends and usually one other day of the
week.  When Parliament is not in session, the Defendant is generally available
in his riding to serve his constituents.  In carrying out these duties the
Defendant spent 464 out of 547 working days for the years 1989, 1990 and 1991
in Ottawa/Hull and Montreal.

8.None
of the documents and witnesses which the Defendant requires for the trial of
this action are found in British Columbia, but rather are found in Ontario or
Quebec or from a jurisdiction outside of Canada.  Accordingly, the
inconvenience to the Defendant and witnesses and the expense of procuring the
attendance of these witnesses would be substantially more if the trial takes
place in British Columbia instead of Ontario.  Furthermore, there is no
material filed by the Plaintiff which suggests that the Plaintiff needs to call
any witnesses or rely upon any documents from British Columbia other than
perhaps a few newspaper reports.

9.The
Defendant filed his Statement of Defence on December 18, 1990.  The action has
proceeded to the stage of each party demanding a list of the other party's
documents.

10.Professor
Raymond Brown, the author of the leading text of defamation law in Canada
entitled
The Law of Defamation in Canada
, sets out in his affidavit
sworn the 10th day of December 1991 the law of defamation in British Columbia
and in Ontario so far as it pertains to this action and is of the opinion that
there are no significant differences between the law of defamation in Ontario
and the law of defamation in British Columbia.  Professor Brown concludes that
if this action were transferred from British Columbia to Ontario the Plaintiff
would not be deprived of any legitimate juridical advantage.

Mr. Wruck, Q.C., counsel for the
defendant, summarizes the defendant's position in support of the application as
follows:

1
.)  Publication originated in
Ottawa, Ontario

2.)Majority
of publications occurred in Ontario and eastern Canada

3.)Witnesses
are in Ontario

4.)Documents
are in Ontario

5.)Defendant
resides in Ontario & Quebec

6.)Plaintiff
resides in London, England

7.)Defendant
is required to be in Ottawa on a regular basis in order to discharge his duties
& responsibilities as a Member of Parliament & as a Member of the Privy
Council

8.)Costs
will be less if action is tried in Ontario

9.)Plaintiff
is not deprived of any juridical or personal advantage if action is tried in
Ontario

10.)No
evidence that parties have any assets in British Columbia

Mr. Christie, counsel for the
plaintiff, replies to the above
seriatim

1.The
plaintiff was in British Columbia at the time the publication came to his
attention.  It was distributed with the clear intent that it would coincide
with the commencement of the plaintiff's speaking tour.

2
.The
fact that the majority of the publications are in Ontario and eastern Canada
does not affect the plaintiff's right to pursue his claim for defamation in
British Columbia.

3
.At
least one witness, in addition to the plaintiff, would be called by the
plaintiff to give evidence as to the effect of the defendant's remarks on him.
The witness Richard Lewers, is a farmer who resides in Sooke, British
Columbia.  He is the president of the Canadian Free Speech League.  He
introduced Mr. Irving at his first speaking engagement in British Columbia.  As
a matter of fact, he read the entire statement to the audience.  Following
that, according to a transcript of this speech, he stated among other things:

The
Canadian Free Speech League rejects emphatically the arogant (sic) smear tactic
of Mr. Weiner.  We are not intimidated by his abuse, nor do we accept his
unfounded comments.  We stand firm for the principles in free speech must be practiced
to be real.  It is only in controversy that the real test of free speech comes.

4
.It
is very doubtful if any witnesses would be called from Ontario.  If the
Holocaust is an issue and are experts are to be called in this respect, the
world's foremost experts reside in the United States and Germany.  None reside
in Ontario nor for that matter in Canada.  Mr. Irving's books are available
anywhere in the world.  There is nothing to indicate that his client's
sympathies and intentions are in Ontario.  None of Mr. Irving's works have
anything to do with Ontario, there is no connection to Ontario.  His works are
involved with what occurred in Europe between 1939 and 1947.

5
.It
is inequitable and unjust to allow a minister of the government to make defamatory
remarks and seek refuge in his residence.  The minister knew that the speaking
tour was to commence on October 27th in Victoria.  He attacked Mr. Irving's
credibility the day before he began to speak.  He cannot throw insults from
Ottawa to British Columbia then say that it is inconvenient for him to come to
British Columbia.

While
Mr. Weiner may be busy now as a Minister of State, the trial is not going to
occur this year and probably not until 1993.  There is no assurance that Mr.
Weiner will be as busy then as he is now.

6
.This
is true.

7
.While
Mr. Weiner may be required to be in Ottawa to carry out his duties, he pleads
privilege as a minster but does not accept the consequences of his statement
made country wide.

8
.There
is no evidence that the costs will be less unless several witnesses are to be
called on behalf of the defendant as alleged in paragraph 3 above of the
defendant's position.

9
.It
is Mr. Irving's right to retain and instruct his counsel of choice.  In this
case, Mr. Christie has had involvement in other cases dealing with the
Holocaust which are well known.  In this respect Mr. Weiner's remarks with
respect to Mr. Irving's "pseudo-historic theories and the web of
myths and distortions by which he seeks to obscure the full horror and
inhumanity of the Nazi regime" makes this defamation action unique in that
respect.  The same facts that will be in issue in this defamation action are
the ones that were in issue in the previous cases tried by Mr. Christie.  Mr.
Christie submits that it is only logical for Mr. Irving to chose him as his
counsel and that that constitutes a personal advantage to him (Irving).

10
.It
makes no difference whether Mr. Irving has assets in British Columbia or not.
There is no evidence that he has any assets in Ontario.

Mr. Wruck replies that it is not
doubted that Mr. Christie has expertise in respect to the matter of the
Holocaust.  He submits however that the defamation action has nothing to do
with the Holocaust; the issue is:  is what the defendant said true or false.
In this respect what is relevant are the facts, documents and persons that Mr.
Weiner relied upon and that these documents are in Ontario and the witnesses
reside there.

It is Mr. Wruck's submission that
there is no nexus between British Columbia as neither the plaintiff nor the
defendant reside here.  The former resides in London, England and the latter
maintains residences in both Ontario and Quebec.

The principles to be applied by a
court exercising its discretion in a
forum non conveniens
application
are set out in
Avenue Properties Ltd.
v.
First City Development

(1986) 7. B.C.L.R. (2d) 45 by Madam Justice McLachlin of the British Columbia
Court of Appeal, now of the Supreme Court of Canada.  These are summarized in
the defendant's argument which I quote:

a.The
decision to refuse or allow an application for a stay is discretionary.  (p.
50)

b.The
plaintiff's choice of forum should not be lightly denied.  He should not be
required to travel outside the jurisdiction in order to present his case,
particularly where he resides in the jurisdiction or where there is
"...some other bona fide connection between the action and the
jurisdiction in which it is sought to be brought".  (p. 50)

c.A
stay should not be granted if there is "...apprehension of prejudice to
one of the parties because of differences in rights, remedies or procedures, in
requiring the action to proceed in another forum...".  (p. 51)

d.The
"modified English rule" set out in
MacShannon
, supra, is the
appropriate test.  (p. 51)

e.The
first branch of the test carries "the connotation that the defendant will
suffer substantial inconvenience
or
injustice."  (p. 52)

f.The
onus is on the defendant in the first branch of the test in
MacShannon
,
supra, that there is another forum to whose jurisdiction the defendant is
amenable and in which justice can be done between the parties at substantially
less inconvenience and expense.  (p. 52)

g.On
the second branch, of the test in
MacShannon
, namely the personal or
juridical advantage, the plaintiff must "show a fair possibility of
gaining an advantage by prosecuting the action in the desired
jurisdiction."  (p. 52)

h.The
onus is on the plaintiff in the second branch of the test in
MacShannon

that the stay will provide the plaintiff with a legitimate personal or
juridical advantage that would be available to him in the court in which he
invoked jurisdiction.  (p. 52)

i.The
matter is a discretionary matter and the courts should not develop an overly
legalistic approach.  (p. 52)

j.The
test involves a balancing of interests - any "advantage to the
plaintiff" as opposed to "any disadvantage to the defendant."
(p. 52)

In
Ecco Heating Products Ltd.

v.
J.K. Campbell and Associates Ltd. et al

(1990)
1990 CanLII 1631 (BC CA)
,
48 B.C.L.R. (2d) 36

Mr. Justice Taylor with Justices Macfarlane and Southin concurring stated at p.
42:

While
the various versions of the test for determining whether a court should grant a
stay of proceedings utilize somewhat different language, I do not believe that
there is a fundamental difference between them.

The
court must consider which forum has the most substantial connection to the
parties and the transaction.  In answering that question it must review all the
factors which connect the parties and the transaction to each jurisdiction.  It
must consider, among other factors, the costs which each would impose on the
parties, the presence of juridical advantage to one party (or disadvantage to
the other) and the law governing the transaction.  Lord Goff said in
Spilada

(at p. 478):

So
it is for connecting factors in this sense that the court must first look; and
these will include not only factors affecting convenience or expense (such as
availability of witnesses), but also other factors such as the law governing
the relevant transaction... and the places where the parties respectively
reside or carry on business.

(e)  If
the court concludes at that stage that there is no other available forum which
is clearly more appropriate for the trial of the action, it will ordinarily
refuse a stay...

(f)  If
however the court concludes at that stage that there is some other available
forum which
prima facie
is clearly more appropriate for the trial of the
action, it will ordinarily grant a stay unless there are circumstances by
reason of which justice requires that a stay should nevertheless not be
granted.

I am
in agreement with the observation of Mr. Justice Hinkson in
First City Invt.
Inc.
that this is consistent with what was said in
Avenue Properties

by Madam Justice McLachlin.

Lord
Goff pointed out in
Spilada
that the requirements which had been set out
by Lord Diplock in
MacShannon
(which ultimately evolved into the test
known as the "modified English rule") were not intended to constitute
an "immutable statement of the law".  Lord Goff said (at p. 475):

...
I do not think that Lord Diplock himself would have regarded this passage as
constituting an immutable statement of the law, but rather as a tentative
statement at an early stage of a period of development... Lord Diplock himself
subsequently recognized that the mere existence of a "legitimate personal
or juridical advantage" of the plaintiff in the English jurisdiction would
not be decisive...

I
think it clear that recent decisions of this court demonstrate that the same
view is taken in this jurisdiction.

[
Spilada
37 [1987] Appeal Court
460:
First City Invts. Inc.
v.
Shrum, Liddle & Hebenton

(1988),
1988 CanLII 2802 (BC CA)
,
26 B.C.L.R. (2d) 46 (C.A.)
- applied
.]

Succinctly put what the court
must consider as indicated by Mr. Justice Taylor in the first portion of the
quotation from his judgment are the following:

1.Which
forum has the most substantial connection to the parties and the transaction.

2.The
costs which each would impose on the parties.

3.The
presence of juridical advantage to one party (a disadvantage to the other).

4.The
law governing the transaction.

5.Other
relevant factors.

The last four of course are the
factors to be considered in determining the answer to the first proposition i.e.
which forum has the most substantial connection to the parties and the
transaction.  Considering which forum has the most substantial connection to
the parties and the transaction, the factors which connect the parties and the
transaction to each jurisdiction, and the principles set out by Madam Justice
McLachlin and in particular the test involving the balance of interests -
"any advantage to the plaintiff" as opposed to "any disadvantage
to the defendant" I conclude that the declaration sought by the defendant
should be granted based on the following:

1.Mr.
Irving, the plaintiff, has no connection whatsoever to British Columbia.  His
only connection is that he was here at the time when the statement came to his
attention.

2.Mr.
Weiner, the defendant, has no connection to British Columbia.  His most
substantial connection is to Ontario where he resides mainly in carrying out
his duties as a member of Parliament and a Minister.  While he may not occupy
either of those positions when the matter comes to trial, the point is that
there is no indication that he would be residing elsewhere than his principle
place of residence in Quebec.  He maintains a temporary residence in the City
of Ottawa according to an Affidavit filed by Neil Drabkin, Barrister and Solicitor,
"... to facilitate his duties and responsibilities as a Minister of the
Crown, a member of the House of commons and as a member of the Queen's Privy
Council."  I am not sure of the exact location of his riding but the
material indicates that he maintains an office in Hull which I take it is in
his riding and which is just across the river from Ottawa.  In any event I
think I have to consider matters as they exist now and not endeavour to take
into account the vagaries of political life which might in the future dictate
that a temporary residence in Ontario is no longer necessary.  It is not the
trial that the court is asked to decline jurisdiction to hear but the entire
proceeding.

3.The
costs of the action in British Columbia far exceed the costs and disbursements
that would be incurred by Mr. Weiner in defending the action in Ontario in view
of the material filed as to the witnesses that Mr. Weiner would wish to call.
The cost in time of course is another factor.

4.Since
Mr. Irving resides in London, England, the costs of his coming to British
Columbia would far exceed the costs of travelling to Ontario.  It would appear
that the number of local (Ontario) witnesses to be called by Mr. Weiner would
exceed the number of local (B.C.) witnesses to be called by Mr. Irving.
Any expert witnesses to be called, according to the material filed, reside in
the United States (I presume in the east) or in Europe.  Here again, the
expense of travelling to Ontario would be less than to British Columbia in these
circumstances.

5.Trying
the action in Ontario does not deprive the plaintiff of any juridical advantage
in view of the factors that I have already stated.  As to the sole personal
advantage referred to i.e. retaining Mr. Christie he would not even be deprived
of those services inasmuch as Mr. Christie has already tried one of the
Holocaust cases in Ontario albeit a criminal case.  Mr. Christie points out
that the practice and procedure in civil matters are different than those in
British Columbia which would place him in at a disadvantage.  However, those
are matters that can be handled by an agent in the Province of Ontario.

6.As
to the law governing the transaction, I quote from the affidavit of Raymond E.
Brown referred to earlier, a professor at the University of Windsor:

....
I authored a two volume treatise on
The Law of Defamation in Canada

(Carswell 1987) (1315pp).  In preparing this treatise, I personally read,
briefed and analyzed almost all of the decisions on libel and slander decided
by Canadian courts in all the common law provinces and the majority of
decisions decided by English, Scottish, Irish, Australian and New Zealand
courts.  I have also reviewed the libel and slander statutes in each of these
jurisdictions as well as all of the principal articles and texts on the law of
defamation.

I
have reviewed the pleadings submitted by both parties in this action.  It is my
opinion that there are no significant differences between the law of Ontario
and the law of British Columbia with respect to the issues raised by these
pleadings.  I conclude, therefore, that if the venue for this action were
transferred from British Columbia to Ontario, the plaintiff, David Irving,
would not be deprived of any legitimate juridical advantage.

He
concludes by stating that the limitation period for such an action in Ontario
is two years.  The limitation period in this case therefore will not expire
until October 26, 1992.

The Surpeme Court of British
Columbia declines jurisdiction in this matter and directs that the proceedings
be stayed.

"K.C.
Murphy, J."

February 21, 1992

Victoria, B.C.
